name: Sarriball
scopeNote: Sarriball as played by Maurizio Sarri's Napoli, 2015-06 to 2018-05 (appointment per The Local 2015-06-12 article, departure confirmed by De Laurentiis per beIN 2018-05-23; exact contractual dates not verified). Sources call it 'Sarriball' / 'Sarri-ball': vertical, high-tempo passing with one-two combinations and third-man runs from a 4-3-3 (started 4-3-1-2 in 2015, switched to 4-3-3 on 2015-09-17), high defensive line and aggressive collective press. 'One-touch' is a loose label; sources stress verticality, triangles and rotations. Zonal marking is asserted in the brief but no mined in-period source states it explicitly (only a zonal-defence reference for Chievo and man-oriented opponents); Sarri's own written stated-view on a 'zonal' label not found. Later Chelsea/Juventus spells are excluded as exemplar evidence. A FanSided piece calls the shape '3-5-2 that seems like a 4-3-3', a minority description.
openQuestions: Marking: no verified in-period source explicitly says 'zonal marking' for Napoli; a search summary of a Spielverlagerung piece says Napoli's zonal press beat Juve's man-oriented press (not mined, unverified). Football-italia 'adl napoli not catenaccio' and calciodangolo Sacchi piece returned 404.
Catalog ids: no manager or team research file for Sarri or Napoli exists. Proposed exemplar ids: manager 'maurizio-sarri' and team 'napoli-sarri-2015-18'.
Dates: start taken from The Local article date 2015-06-12; end from beIN article date 2018-05-23 (De Laurentiis confirmation); second-source check not done.
Sarri's primary quotes on his own principles (verticality, 'play on the ground') were not found as dated interviews; Jorginho quote on Sarri's style is only seen in Sky Sports, not a primary source.
FanSided describes the shape as '3-5-2 that often seems like a 4-3-3', which conflicts with all other sources (4-3-3 with a temporary back three in build-up).

sources.title: Maurizio Sarri: Coach Watch - Coaches' Voice
sources.evidence: Sarri's increased time at Napoli – he spent three seasons there – meant that his 4-3-3 evolved further than it did at Chelsea.

sources.title: Maurizio Sarri: Coach Watch - Coaches' Voice
sources.evidence: They were particularly fluid towards the left (above), where they regularly progressed possession via quick combinations and rotations and runs from a third player. Faouzi Ghoulam advanced from left-back, and the right-footed Dries Mertens or Lorenzo Insigne, as their left-sided forward, drifted infield

sources.title: Maurizio Sarri: Coach Watch - Coaches' Voice
sources.evidence: Towards the right they were considerably more direct; José Callejón, as their right-sided forward, attacked around the outside of opponents to provide crosses or, if play was unfolding towards the left, moved infield to operate alongside Higuaín as a second striker.

sources.title: Maurizio Sarri: Coach Watch - Coaches' Voice
sources.evidence: Jorginho also orchestrated a significant amount of their deeper build-up and linked play to both sides of the pitch, and his speed of thought and passing range contributed to the extent to which they dictated play before their rotations and movements unfolded.

sources.title: Maurizio Sarri: Coach Watch - Coaches' Voice
sources.evidence: Sarri’s Napoli applied a particularly aggressive press that often resembled the shape of Chelsea's. The younger Higuaín, and later Mertens, worked across the pitch to press the in-possession central defender, and attempted the direct their pressure wide to prevent switches of play and to force possession to one side of the pitch

sources.title: Maurizio Sarri: Coach Watch - Coaches' Voice
sources.evidence: With the opposition's defenders under pressure from Napoli's striker, the closest attacking central midfielder and wide forward moved from their opponents to adopt half-and-half positions so that they could block passes through midfield while remaining close enough to those opponents to press them, if required.

sources.title: Maurizio Sarri: Coach Watch - Coaches' Voice
sources.evidence: Napoli, like Chelsea, regularly recorded a strong grasp of possession, and therefore made numerous regains via their counter-press and the ability of those offering cover to make regains after attacking players had conceded the ball in the final third

sources.title: Maurizio Sarri: Coach Watch - Coaches' Voice
sources.evidence: His players' familiarity with his methods meant Sarri's team accumulating a club record 91 points in Serie A – the most of any runner up in the competition's history.

sources.title: Analysing SarriBall (Get Italian Football News)
sources.evidence: Allan was deployed in a box-to-box role, though his attributes are typically more suited to that of a holding midfielder (remind you of anyone?). However, Allan was instructed to win the ball high up the pitch and was given the freedom to use his tenacity and instinctive hunger to win the ball in the areas he saw fit to do so, covered by Jorginho sitting deeper

sources.title: Analysing SarriBall (Get Italian Football News)
sources.evidence: Typically the full- backs almost played as wing-backs, providing the width as Jose Callejon and Lorenzo Insige drove inside to support Dries Mertens, creating overloads against defenders, ready to execute one-twos and even pick up the ball in ‘number 10’ areas.

sources.title: Analysing SarriBall (Get Italian Football News)
sources.evidence: Under Sarri, Napoli scored a total of 251 league goals – more than Juventus’ 238 tally – and achieved the top three on every occasion, twice finishing runners up

sources.title: What is Sarriball? (Breaking the Lines)
sources.evidence: From 2015 to 2018, Sarri's Napoli became widely recognized for its unique style of play predicated upon verticality in possession, high-tempo passing, and circuit-based football. His team typically utilised third-man runs to either draw defenders out of position, provide a clear option for progression, or break through the opposition's defensive block.

sources.title: What is Sarriball? (Breaking the Lines)
sources.evidence: In order to play with the necessary levels of verticality, Sarri employed a 4-3-3, which created diamonds and triangles across the pitch that could easily be manufactured and worked on in training.

sources.title: What is Sarriball? (Breaking the Lines)
sources.evidence: When the opportunity comes about by moving the opposition into wider spaces through press baiting (drawing the opposition out using short passes deeper in the pitch), the goalkeeper would play a long ball through the middle of the pitch into one of the attacking players sitting between the lines

sources.title: What is Sarriball? (Breaking the Lines)
sources.evidence: Sarri's Napoli scored their first goal using a similar idea. The four defenders circulate the ball against Real Madrid in order to draw the Real players towards them. Once the Real players start to press, Kalidou Koulibaly at left-centre back plays a vertical pass to Dries Mertens

sources.title: What is Sarriball? (Breaking the Lines)
sources.evidence: despite Sarri using the same rough formation at both Chelsea and Napoli the majority of the time (4-3-3), his teams would be able to play in a 3-2-5, a 3-1-6, or a 2-3-5

sources.title: What is Sarriball? (Breaking the Lines)
sources.evidence: At both Chelsea and Napoli, there was an onus on one of the midfielders or one of the fullbacks, depending in the position of the ball and opposition, to create a back three in the build-up when Sarri came up against teams playing a two up-top formation

sources.title: What is Sarriball? (Breaking the Lines)
sources.evidence: This is also why Sarri prefers to have goalkeepers who are very confident with the ball at their feet.

sources.title: Sarri’s tactical revolution at Napoli (FanSided)
sources.evidence: Napoli’s style of play under Sarri involves playing a high defensive line, with lots of possession and constant ball movement through the use of both triangle and vertical passing.

sources.title: Sarri’s tactical revolution at Napoli (FanSided)

sources.title: Sarri’s Napoli in rampant home victory (Spielverlagerung)
sources.evidence: One of the biggest offensive characteristics of Sarri’s Napoli is using central progressions to create space in wider areas. This takes advantage of the inevitable pressure that follows a vertical progression. Opponents naturally collapse on the ball in reaction to vertical passes

sources.title: Sarri’s Napoli in rampant home victory (Spielverlagerung)
sources.evidence: This movement is in line with a general rule Sarri has instilled, namely; players who are covered move forwards whilst a nearby team-mate drops.

sources.title: Sarri’s Napoli in rampant home victory (Spielverlagerung)
sources.evidence: Players moving in opposite directions can be a great tool to disrupt man-oriented opponents since it challenges the nearby defenders to co-ordinate their marking in a short space of time.
